acl.description:
List of ACL entries. Each entry must contain tag_type and permissions; qualifier is required only for user/group entries. Entry types: user, group, mask, other. Qualifiers may be usernames, group names, or numeric IDs (decimal). Permissions are 3-char strings like 'rwx', 'rw-', 'r--', '---'. The 'mask' entry is mandatory when user/group entries exist, optional otherwise. Entries must follow POSIX validity rules (exactly one user_obj, group_obj, other; unique qualifiers per type). See acl(5) manpage for details on valid ACL construction and semantics. Comment lines (starting with #) are NOT supported in this short-text representation (long form supports comments, but this template uses short-text one-line-per-entry format as canonical). Example: user::rw-, group::r--, other::r--, mask::rwx, user:alice:rwx, group:devs:r--. For default ACLs, this file would represent the access ACL (same format); default ACLs are stored in filesystem extended attributes, not in a separate config file — this template is for textual ACL representation (e.g., used by getfacl/setfacl roundtrips or scripts). However, per the acl(5) manpage, a default ACL may be empty (zero entries) and is valid — so empty list is allowed to represent no default ACL. The file is typically not directly edited; used for scripting (setfacl -f). See acl_set_file(3) and acl_from_text(3). This template does NOT include file path or object type — it represents only the ACL text form entries as a list. To apply, pipe to setfacl -f or use acl_set_file(3). This is NOT a system config file like /etc/fstab — it's an ACL specification file, e.g., 'acl.txt' used in backup/restore or provisioning scripts, matching getfacl output short format (without comments). However, per the prompt: 'package/service: acl' and 'production-sane config file' — the canonical config representation is the text ACL itself. So the config file is an ACL text specification file (one entry per line, colon-separated, as generated by getfacl -s and accepted by setfacl -f). See getfacl(1): '-s, --skip-access' prints only the ACL text form without other info, which matches this template. This file is used to store/recreate ACLs outside filesystem extended attributes (e.g., in configuration management). Per acl(5), ACLs are stored in filesystem extended attributes, but for config management purposes, a textual ACL file (one per object) is a common practice. So this template defines that textual ACL file format (one entry per line, short form). Example valid file: user::rw-
group::r--
mask::r--
other::r--
user:alice:rwx (but note: if user/group present, mask is required — this template does not enforce validity; caller must provide valid ACL). Also per acl(5), when entries like user:alice:rwx are present without mask, the file is invalid. To support real-world usage (e.g., scripts that generate/apply ACLs), allow mask omission only when no user/group entries (acl(5): 'If an ACL contains no entries of ACL_USER or ACL_GROUP tag types, the ACL_MASK entry is optional'). We enforce validity via values_schema description, not template. Template is format-only. See getfacl(1) short format examples. Note: getfacl -s uses short form (comma-separated in some outputs) but getfacl -s -n outputs long-form-like entries (one per line). This template matches the one-entry-per-line format (like getfacl output with comments stripped), which is standard for scripts (e.g., 'setfacl -f acl.txt'). See setfacl(1): 'If -f is given, the ACLs are read from file'. So this is a scriptable ACL file format (one entry per line). This is not a runtime config file like /etc/acl.conf — there is no such standard file; ACLs are filesystem metadata. But for configuration management (Ansible, etc.), the common practice is to manage ACLs via text files containing one entry per line. Therefore, the config file is this ACL specification file (text ACL). See also: acl(5) 'ACL TEXT FORMS' short/long forms. We choose long-form style without comments (one entry per line) for readability in scripts. Template uses Jinja2 one-entry-per-line format matching getfacl long form without comments (no # prefix). getfacl --omit-header --absolute-names --omit-wall --numeric --out-mask --skip-access outputs long form (one entry per line) — this is what we mimic, but without comments. So template: user::rw-

We output one per line for clarity. Template directive: {{ entry.tag_type }}{% if entry.qualifier is defined and entry.qualifier != '' %}:{{ entry.qualifier }}{% endif %}:{{ entry.permissions }}. This matches user:alice:rw- etc. Qualifier can be numeric ID (e.g., '1000') — we allow that via string type. Permissions: 'rwx', 'rw-', etc. — string, exactly 3 chars of [rwx-]. values_schema.description: ACL tag type. Must be one of 'user', 'group', 'mask', 'other'. For ACL_USER_OBJ and ACL_GROUP_OBJ, use tag_type 'user' or 'group' with empty qualifier (output as '::'). For ACL_USER, 'user' with qualifier (e.g., 'alice'). For ACL_GROUP, 'group' with qualifier. mask and other never have qualifiers (use empty qualifier, output as '::'). Validity: exactly one user_obj, group_obj, other; unique qualifiers per type; mask required if any user/group entries present (see acl(5)).

qualifier.description: User or group identifier (name or decimal number). Empty for user_obj, group_obj, mask, other. Required for ACL_USER and ACL_GROUP entries. If empty, template outputs '::'; if non-empty, template outputs ':' + qualifier + ':'. Example: 'alice', '1000', 'devs', '1001'.

permissions.description: Three-character permission string. Each character is r, w, x, or - (dash). Order: read, write, execute/search. Example: 'rwx', 'rw-', 'r--', '---'. Must be consistent with tag type (e.g., execute for directories/files as appropriate), but validity is caller's responsibility per acl(5).
